title: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: Our method reaches equal or higher accuracy than every baseline at lower cost, sitting on the Pareto frontier across model families.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, accuracy vs log-cost scatter, dashed Pareto line
description: Two side-by-side scatter plots titled 'Gemini models' and 'GPT models'. The y-axis is UNMET F1 (0.5 to 0.9+). The x-axis is model API cost per dataset pass in USD, on a log scale from 5 to 200. Each point has a vertical 95% confidence-interval bar and a model-name label. Colors and markers separate methods: blue circles for Gandalf, gold triangles for Archipelago, green squares for Agent-as-a-Judge, orange diamonds for AutoRubric. Filled markers mean 3 evaluations per task and hollow markers mean 1. A dashed gray line joins the Pareto-optimal points. Blue Gandalf points sit highest and farthest left, so the frontier runs through them. The baselines lie lower and to the right. A legend sits at the bottom.
caption: UNMET F1 and model API cost per pass on \benchmarkabbrev\ (24 tasks), grouped by backing-model family. Dashed lines connect the Pareto-optimal configurations in each panel based on point estimates. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals from resampling tasks; they do not separately estimate variation between repeated evaluations. AutoRubric with GPT-5.4 was stopped early because of cost. For Gandalf, per-pass cost reflects token use, not per-token price alone: Gemini 3.8 Flash made about $1.5\times$ as many LLM calls as Gemini 3.1 Pro, with larger contexts and more reasoning per call.
abstract: As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.
